title: Encapsulation MTU path blackhole - oncall playbook (draft)
content:
Summary:

Short: Some customer private deployments have seen intermittent control-plane RPC failures and agent reconnect loops. Root condition appears to be an MTU/path-MTU blackhole introduced when tenant traffic is encapsulated (geneve/ipsec) and then inspected/rewritten by customer firewall/DPI boxes that drop or fragment large encapsulated packets.

Impact:
- Symptoms seen in multiple customers: control-plane RPC timeouts, pod-agent reconnects, degraded telemetry flushes, occasional bursts of 502s for model invoke requests routed via private connector.
- Frequency: intermittent under higher concurrency / when large KV-cache payloads are returned (long model responses).
- Customer-visible: short flaps (10-120s) where private agent cannot reach control plane, then recovers after TCP retransmit/backoff.

Timeline (high level):
- 2027-03-02 11:05 UTC: First alert — control-plane RPC error rate up for customer A
- 2027-03-02 11:07 UTC: Oncall collected pcap from edge and saw consistent MSS reduction then sudden SYN retries
- 2027-03-02 11:12 UTC: Temporary workaround applied (lowered MTU on tunnel endpoint) — errors reduced
- 2027-03-02 11:40 UTC: Customer reported DPI firmware upgrade coincident with onset

Hypothesis:
- Encapsulation increases packet size beyond path MTU. Firewall/DPI box in customer's on-prem path either:
  1) silently drops large encapsulated packets, or
  2) rewrites headers in a way that breaks fragmentation checks, causing downstream devices to discard fragments, or
  3) performs deep inspection and fragments/reassembles in a non-standard way that breaks TCP MSS heuristics.
- Under increased concurrency we hit larger packets (TLS stacks + gRPC + KV caches + encapsulation), thus tripping the blackhole.

Evidence collected:
- PCAP from edge: lots of repeated SYNs, then occasional ICMP fragmentation-needed (but not always), and gaps where sequence numbers jump on retransmit.
- Customer firewall logs: shows drops for "large UDP fragments" around the time window (configurable threshold).
- Reproduced in lab by creating a geneve tunnel and adding an iptables rule to drop fragments >1400 bytes — caused identical control-plane RPC retry patterns.
- Telemetry: spike in retransmits seen from host-level netstat/snmp counters correlated with model-response size.

Immediate mitigations (oncall playbook):
1) Identification
   - Check the control-plane error dashboard + agent status for the customer. Note times and affected agents.
   - Retrieve edge pcap: tcpdump -n -s 0 -w /tmp/egress.pcap host <agent-ip> and filter for SYN/RETRY/ICMP.
   - Query agent logs for gRPC error codes (UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED).

2) Short-term fixes (apply one at a time, monitor):
   - Lower tunnel MTU on the private connector endpoint by 40-80 bytes (example: ip link set dev tun0 mtu 1400). This avoids fragmentation but reduces throughput.
   - Enable TCP MSS clamping on the tunnel egress (if supported on customer's firewall or our router): iptables --table mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu
   - If using geneve/vxlan, reduce outer_header_size assumption in agent config to explicitly clamp inner MSS.
   - As emergency, throttle large model responses via our routing layer to avoid generating > path-MTU packets (configuration flag in connector: max_payload_bytes_for_rpc).

3) Communication
   - Notify customer SRE and security contact with observed PCAP excerpt + suggested firewall config change (MSS clamping or allow fragments).
   - Open a ticket with firewall vendor if logs indicate firmware bug (include captured hex + timestamps).

4) Monitoring after mitigation
   - Watch retransmit rate and control-plane RPC success rates for 30 mins.
   - Keep pcap rolling for 10 mins post change to validate no further fragment drops.

Longer-term fixes / follow-ups (action items):
- Default: add MSS clamp to our private connector images and add automated health check that validates path MTU at connection startup (send PMTUD probe and measure).
- Add explicit fragmentation detection telemetry: count "out-of-order" sequence ranges and presence/absence of ICMP messages.
- Make connector fallback degrade model payload size instead of failing requests when fragmentation is observed.
- Run a compatibility matrix for common customer firewalls (Palo Alto, Fortinet, Cisco, Checkpoint) to document known behaviours around encapsulated fragment handling.
- Add e2e lab harness where we can intentionally drop fragments to validate our runbooks.

Runbook: exact commands and checks for oncall
- Quick health checks:
  - curl -sS https://console.internal.redwood/api/agents/<customer>/status | jq .
  - kubectl logs -n private-connectors <connector-pod> --since=15m | grep -E "(gRPC|timeout|UNAVAILABLE|retransmit)"
- Collect pcaps:
  - tcpdump -i eth0 host <agent-ip> and port <controlplane-port> -w /tmp/egress.pcap
  - w/ tshark: tshark -r /tmp/egress.pcap -Y "tcp.analysis.retransmission or icmp.type==3" -V > /tmp/pcap-analysis.txt
- Packet inspection hints:
  - Look for "Fragmented IP datagram" lines and check outer_headers (geneve/vxlan + inner IP header).
  - Note if ICMP type 3 code 4 (Fragmentation needed) is present — path PMTUD sometimes suppressed on middleboxes.
- Quick workaround (apply on our side if customer operator cannot change config immediately):
  - ip link set dev <tun> mtu 1360 && restart connector service
  - or add iptables TCPMSS clamp as above (quick to revert)
- Rollback steps:
  - Restore previous MTU and clear iptables mangle rule. Monitor for reappearance.

Replication steps (lab):
1) Create two VMs with a geneve tunnel between them.
2) Place an nginx-based "firewall" VM in between with tc/iptables rules to drop fragments or drop UDP > X bytes, or install an L7 DPI demo that re-fragments.
3) Run a gRPC service that returns large payloads (2-4KB) and run agent to invoke service concurrently. Observe retransmits and RPC failures.
4) Test mitigations: lower MTU / enable MSS clamp and verify recovered behavior.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Is there a way to detect this gracefully from the agent before control-plane requests fail (early PMTUD validation)?
- Should we proactively advertise a smaller MSS on initial handshake from agent when in encapsulated mode?
- Does any customer hardware rewrite outer headers in a way that alters IP ID/DF flags? (we've seen logs indicating DF toggles)

Notes to self (informal):
- Customer B had similar pattern but blamed BGP; after we lowered MTU at connector the symptoms stopped — maybe multiple customers have same root cause.
- Avoid telling customer to disable DPI — instead ask for MSS clamp or fragment allowlist.

Post-incident tickets and owners:
- RED-4821: egress mtu blackhole triage (owner: Samir)
- RED-4902: connector image: default MSS clamp and PMTUD probe (owner: Marta)
- RED-4903: create lab harness for fragment-drop tests (owner: Jonas)

References / links:
- RFC 1191 / RFC 8201 notes on PMTUD
- internal pcap analysis gist: https://gist.github.com/redwood/pcap-egress-mtu-2027

If you're oncall and see this pattern: prioritize quick MTU/MSS clamp changes and capture pcaps. Don't escalate to networking infra immediately unless changes don't help within 20min. This is disruptive but generally fixable with MTU/MSS adjustments.

End of draft — still rough, needs diagrams (flow of encapsulation->firewall->fragment) and a one-click connector config to flip mtu/clamp.
